content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem focused on the 7-minute latency spike on io-shop caused by slow responses from the pricing dependency, resolved by a restart, noting the error rate barely rose so the real impact was latency. I need to be careful not to conflate Argus's hold time with actual outage duration or misrepresent the impact figures.

I should also flag the assumptions clearly: the restart's effectiveness was inferred from timing correlation rather than proven, the root cause inside the pricing service itself was never actually investigated, and the pre-existing ClientDisconnected errors were treated as unrelated background noise without confirmation. The executive summary should stay high-level — account and basket pages were slow — while the root cause section notes basket-total calls to the pricing service took around 1500ms, with the underlying cause left undetermined.

assumptions: The restart of io-pricing was credited with the recovery because the service returned to baseline within ~40 seconds of it; this is timing correlation, not proof — a transient condition in io-pricing could have cleared on its own.

io-pricing was treated as an internally-owned dependency (checkout-platform) on the strength of the service register entry. The alternative reading — that it fronts a third party — was considered and set aside, not tested.
No io-pricing logs, metrics or resource data were pulled. The conclusion that the fault originated there rests entirely on io-shop's client-side WARN logs reporting slow upstream calls.

The recurring ClientDisconnected errors on the account page appear before the onset as well as during it, and were treated as pre-existing background noise (shoppers abandoning slow or unwanted page loads) rather than a symptom of this incident.

Absence of a deploy or flag change was inferred from the change-event and flag-provider queries returning nothing for the window searched; changes outside that window, or changes made outside those systems, would not have been visible.
Recovery is judged from io-shop's own latency and error metrics returning to baseline; no independent check was made that io-pricing itself was healthy afterwards, so a recurrence is possible.
input.executive_summary:
Between 22:08 and 22:15 UTC on 25 September 2026, the online shop's account and basket pages became very slow to load. Pages that normally return in a fraction of a second were taking around a second and a half, because an internal service that calculates basket totals stopped responding promptly. Shoppers using those pages during the window would have seen long waits; some closed the page before it finished loading. The proportion of requests that outright failed stayed close to its normal level throughout — this was a slowness incident rather than an outage, and the shop remained available.

Automated monitoring raised an alert at 22:13, an automated investigation identified the slow internal dependency within about a minute, and the dependency was restarted at 22:14. Response times returned to normal by 22:15 and were confirmed recovered shortly after. A draft code change has since been proposed for review to make the shop more resilient to this dependency being slow. The underlying reason the pricing component slowed down has not yet been determined and needs follow-up with the team that owns it.
input.root_cause: Starting at 22:08 UTC, the internally-owned pricing service (pricing.io-internal.svc, io-pricing, owned by checkout-platform) began taking ~1500ms to answer io-shop's /basket-total calls — first for a fraction of requests, then for essentially all of them — which dragged io-shop's p50/p95 latency from roughly 45ms/210ms to roughly 1500ms/1700ms. No deploy, config or feature-flag change was recorded for io-shop in the preceding hours and its memory and request volume were flat, so the fault arrived entirely through the dependency rather than from io-shop itself; restarting io-pricing at 22:14 cleared it and io-shop was back at baseline by 22:15. Why io-pricing degraded was not established — no io-pricing-side logs or metrics were examined, so the restart resolved the symptom without identifying the defect behind it.
